title: Passive and impersonal constructions
objectives: I can explain why every accent mark and every spelling pattern in the words of this unit is written the way it is.
I can build and read the passive with ser plus a participle and por, and make the participle agree with its subject.
I can use se as a passive and as an impersonal marker, and decide between them by asking whether the verb has a direct object.
I can tell an event from the state it leaves, with ser plus a participle against estar plus a participle.
I can talk about unspecified people with the third person plural, a gente and você, and read everyday signs, notices and news headlines.

vocabulary.note: The large title at the top of a front page or a news site. The syllable man is nasal because the n closes it, ch is [ʃ] as in chuva, and the t before the weak final e is said [tʃ].

example.pt: A manchete do jornal fala sobre a nova lei.
example.en: The newspaper headline is about the new law.
example.literal: The headline of-the newspaper speaks about the new law.

vocabulary.note: An official announcement issued by a company or an authority. It is the participle of comunicar (to communicate) used as a noun: the thing that was communicated.

example.pt: O comunicado foi divulgado pela empresa ontem à noite.
example.en: The statement was released by the company last night.
example.literal: The statement was released by-the company yesterday at-the night.

vocabulary.note: Also a warning. A written aviso is posted on a door or a wall. Avisar is the verb, to notify or to warn.

example.pt: Um aviso foi colado na porta do prédio.
example.en: A notice was stuck on the door of the building.
example.literal: A notice was glued on-the door of-the building.

vocabulary.note: Any flat plate: a street sign, a memorial plaque and a car's license plate are all placas. Está escrito (is written) is how Brazilians say what a sign or a text says.

example.pt: Na placa está escrito que é proibido fumar.
example.en: The sign says that smoking is forbidden.
example.literal: On-the sign is written that is forbidden to-smoke.

vocabulary.note: A written set of rules for a building, a school or an organization. Condomínio names a building whose residents jointly own the common areas and pay a monthly fee (the fee is also called condomínio), and the assembleia is the residents' meeting.

example.pt: O regulamento do condomínio foi aprovado na assembleia.
example.en: The building's regulations were approved at the meeting.
example.literal: The regulation of-the condominium was approved in-the assembly.

vocabulary.note: One syllable: ei is a diphthong said like the ay of day. The plural is leis.

example.pt: A nova lei será votada na próxima semana.
example.en: The new law will be voted on next week.
example.literal: The new law will-be voted in-the next week.

vocabulary.note: A money penalty. Pagar multa is to pay a fine.

example.pt: A multa é cobrada junto com a conta de luz.
example.en: The fine is charged together with the electricity bill.
example.literal: The fine is charged together with the bill of light.

vocabulary.note: A time limit for doing something. Inscrição (enrollment, registration) is explained in the spelling notes: the cedilla and the ão ending.

example.pt: O prazo para a inscrição termina na sexta-feira.
example.en: The registration deadline ends on Friday.
example.literal: The deadline for the enrollment ends in-the Friday.

vocabulary.note: A participle used as an adjective, from proibir. On signs it stands alone before an infinitive: Proibido estacionar. After é it is followed directly by an infinitive, which acts as the subject: É proibido fumar says that the act of smoking is forbidden.

example.pt: É proibido estacionar na frente da garagem.
example.en: Parking in front of the garage is forbidden.
example.literal: Is forbidden to-park in front of-the garage.

vocabulary.note: The opposite of proibido, built the same way: the participle of permitir.

example.pt: Neste parque é permitido andar de bicicleta.
example.en: In this park, riding a bicycle is allowed.
example.literal: In-this park is permitted to-walk of bicycle.

vocabulary.note: Used for the ceremonial opening of a building, a road, a bridge or a shop. The au is a diphthong [aw], and the g before u is the hard g, so gu here is [gu].

example.pt: O novo hospital foi inaugurado pelo governador.
example.en: The new hospital was inaugurated by the governor.

vocabulary.note: The n closes the first syllable, so fun is a nasal syllable. The accent of jesuítas is explained in the spelling notes.

example.pt: A cidade de São Paulo foi fundada por jesuítas.
example.en: The city of São Paulo was founded by Jesuits.

vocabulary.note: The noun is a invenção. Século has an accent because it is stressed on the third to last syllable.

example.pt: O telefone foi inventado no século dezenove.
example.en: The telephone was invented in the nineteenth century.
example.literal: The telephone was invented in-the century nineteen.

vocabulary.note: Built from des (un-) plus cobrir (to cover), so to discover is to take the cover off. The participle is irregular: descoberto, like coberto and aberto. In des-co-brir the s ends its syllable and is said [s], and the c before o is [k].

example.pt: A doença foi descoberta por um médico brasileiro.
example.en: The disease was discovered by a Brazilian doctor.

vocabulary.note: The participle construído has an accent on the í because the u and the í are two separate syllables (a hiatus): cons-tru-Í-do. The feminine is construída.

example.pt: A ponte foi construída pelos operários em dois anos.
example.en: The bridge was built by the workers in two years.

vocabulary.note: Also the verb for passing an exam: Fui aprovado no exame is I passed the exam, literally I was approved in-the exam. Os aprovados are the people who passed.

example.pt: O projeto foi aprovado por quase todos os deputados.
example.en: The bill was approved by almost all the representatives.

vocabulary.note: Used for releasing news, lists and results. It comes from Latin vulgus, the common people, the root of English divulge and vulgar.

example.pt: A lista dos aprovados foi divulgada hoje de manhã.
example.en: The list of successful candidates was released this morning.
example.literal: The list of-the approved was spread today of morning.

vocabulary.note: Nouns in -ção name the act or result of a verb: inventar gives invenção. The ç is [s] before ã, and the nasal diphthong ão is stressed, so no further accent is needed. The plural is invenções.

example.pt: A invenção do avião mudou o mundo.
example.en: The invention of the airplane changed the world.

vocabulary.note: Also a work of art or literature. Obras in the plural, or em obras on a sign, means roadworks or construction in progress.

example.pt: A rua está interditada por causa de uma obra.
example.en: The street is closed off because of roadworks.
example.literal: The street is interdicted by cause of a work.

vocabulary.note: A participle used as an adjective, from interditar (compare English interdict): closed by an authority such as the police or the city hall, for example after an accident or a fire. Portuguese says está interditado desde, with the present of estar, where English says has been closed off since.

example.pt: O prédio está interditado desde o incêndio.
example.en: The building has been closed off since the fire.
example.literal: The building is interdicted since the fire.

vocabulary.note: From vago, vacant. It names an empty place that someone can take: a job, a parking space, a seat, a place in a school.

example.pt: Aluga-se vaga de garagem perto do metrô.
example.en: Garage space for rent near the subway.
example.literal: Rents-itself vacancy of garage near of-the subway.

vocabulary.note: From morar, to live somewhere. The feminine is a moradora.

example.pt: Os moradores foram avisados sobre a falta de água.
example.en: The residents were told about the water outage.
example.literal: The dwellers were warned about the lack of water.

vocabulary.note: Also personal property and assets. Patrimônio da humanidade is the Portuguese name for World Heritage. The accent is explained in the spelling notes.

example.pt: O centro histórico foi declarado patrimônio da humanidade.
example.en: The historic center was declared a World Heritage Site.
example.literal: The historic center was declared heritage of-the humanity.

vocabulary.note: Also to demand. The x is [z] because ex comes before a vowel. After exigir que the verb is in the subjunctive: sejam is the present subjunctive of ser, and entregues is the short participle of entregar.

example.pt: O regulamento exige que os documentos sejam entregues no prazo.
example.en: The regulations require the documents to be handed in on time.
example.literal: The regulation demands that the documents be delivered in-the deadline.

dialogues.title: The building meeting
dialogues.context: The building manager, Seu Paulo, talks with two residents, Dona Lúcia and Bruno, about a notice on the elevator door. Seu is a familiar short form of senhor, and Dona is the matching title for a woman.

lines.literal: Good night. You-all saw the notice that was glued on-the door of-the elevator?

lines.pt: Três dias. O serviço será feito pela mesma empresa do ano passado.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: accents and stress in the words of this unit
grammar.explanation:
This unit has many accented words because news, law and history use long words, and long words are where the stress rules do their work. None of the marks is arbitrary. Each one comes out of the procedure from the stress lesson: divide the word into syllables, find the stressed syllable by ear, read the default from the ending, and write an accent only if the stress disagrees with the default. The mark you write is then chosen by the vowel: the acute for an open vowel (or for i and u, which have only one quality), the circumflex for a closed vowel. Before m or n the vowel is nasal and the mark is a convention: the circumflex in the middle of a word (Antônio, trânsito) and the acute in words ending in em or ens (também, parabéns). The tilde has a different job, which is to make a vowel nasal.

The default, restated: words ending in a, e or o (with or without s), am, em or ens are stressed on the second to last syllable, and words ending in anything else, including ã and ão, are stressed on the last. A word that obeys its default needs no mark, which is why confiança (con-fi-AN-ça), inaugurado, interditado and proibido have none. The words in this unit that do carry a mark fall into five groups, and each group is one way of breaking the default.

Group 1, stress on the last syllable although the ending predicts the second to last. Está (es-TÁ), será, dá, já, lá and há end in a; também and alguém end in em; você and vocês end in e and es; metrô ends in o. All of them need a mark. One-syllable words follow the same logic: é, só and três are stressed and end in e, o or es, so they are written with a mark, while the small word e (and) is weak and has none. That is the whole difference between é (is) and e (and), and between está (is) and esta (this). Né is não é said fast, and it keeps the open vowel of é.

Group 2, the tilde endings. The endings ã, ão and ãos default to the last syllable, and the tilde already marks the nasal vowel, so nothing more is written: então (en-TÃO), avião, aviação, reunião, invenção, inscrição, construção, estão, são, vão, não, amanhã, manhã, irmã, irmãos. One word breaks even this default: órgão is ÓR-gão, stressed on the second to last, so it carries an acute as well as the tilde.

Group 3, stress on the third to last syllable. No ending predicts this, so a mark is always written: século, histórico, urbanístico, público, última, próxima, rígidas, trânsito. The vowel decides the mark. Século and histórico have an open stressed vowel, so the acute; última, público and rígidas take the acute because u and i have only one quality. In trânsito the stressed a is nasal before the n, and in the middle of a word the convention for a stressed nasal a, e or o before m or n is the circumflex, as in câmera and lâmpada from the stress lesson.

Group 4, words that end in a glide plus a vowel: ia, io, ua, uo, ea, eo and their plurals. For the stress rule Portuguese counts the i or u as a syllable of its own, so notícia is no-TÍ-ci-a, stressed on the third to last, and must be marked. The same reasoning marks experiência, conferência, independência, distâncias, cerimônia, condomínio, patrimônio, incêndio, Brasília, funcionários, operários, edifícios, área, rádio, relatório, palácio, prédio, Lúcio, Antônio and água. The mark again follows the vowel: ê, â and ô before n (experiência, incêndio, distâncias, patrimônio, cerimônia, Antônio), the acute elsewhere (notícia, área, rádio, relatório, prédio). Compare confiança, where the a is a true final vowel and the word is stressed on the second to last by default, and tia, where the stressed vowel is the i itself.

Group 5, a stressed i or u that must not merge with the vowel before it. In país (pa-ÍS), jesuítas (je-su-Í-tas) and construído and construída (cons-tru-Í-do) the two vowels are a hiatus, that is, two syllables, and the accent on the í says so. Without it the pair would be read as a diphthong, as ui is in fui. No accent is needed when l, m, n, r, z or nh follows in the same syllable (ruim, juiz, raiz).

One more mark is not about stress. The grave accent of à and às is the crase from the places lesson: the preposition a fused with the article a, as in ontem à noite (last night, literally yesterday at-the night). Há (there is, or ago, as in há três anos) is a Group 1 word; its accent also separates it from the preposition a.

Not every long word takes a mark. Assembleia is as-sem-BLEI-a: it ends in a, so the default is the second to last syllable, which is the ei, and no mark is needed. Before 2009 it was written assembléia, but the agreement removed the acute from the open ei and oi of words stressed on the second to last.

Worked example, patrimônio. Divide it: pa-tri-mô-ni-o. The ending io is a glide plus a vowel, so the i counts as its own syllable and the stress falls on the third to last, mô. No ending predicts that, so a mark is required. The stressed o is followed by n, so it is closed, and the mark is the circumflex: ô. Because accents belong to a particular form and not to a whole word family, they can be recomputed: construir has none, but its participle construído needs its í because of the hiatus.

Ending em defaults to second to last; stress is last
Ending a defaults to second to last; stress is last
Stressed one-syllable word ending in e, so it takes a mark; the plain conjunction e (and) is weak and takes none
Ending o defaults to second to last; stress is last; closed vowel
Ending ão defaults to last; the tilde alone is enough
Stress is second to last although ão defaults to last; acute added
Third to last; open vowel gives the acute
Third to last; a before n is closed, so the circumflex
Ending ia counts as two syllables, so the stress is third to last
Same reason; o before n is closed, so the circumflex
Hiatus: the accent keeps a and i in separate syllables

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: consonants and letter groups in the words of this unit
grammar.explanation:
Portuguese spelling is a code in which something you can see decides the sound: the letter that comes next, the position in the word, or a mark. This note reads the rest of the unit's new words with that code. The table lists each pattern once, with words from the vocabulary, the dialogues and the reading.

The cedilla. The letter c is [k] before a, o and u, and [s] before e and i. To write [s] before a, o or u, Portuguese adds a cedilla: ç. That is why inscrição, invenção, construção, calçada, começada, março, serviço, doença and confiança have one, and why cerimônia, notícia, edifício, conferência and independência have none: their c is already before e or i. A ç never begins a word. The ending -ção is the ordinary way to turn a verb into a noun naming the act or the result (inventar, invenção; construir, construção; inscrever, inscrição). It is said [sɐ̃w̃], with the nasal diphthong you met in pão, and it is stressed on its last syllable. The plural is -ções: invenções, construções.

Digraphs, meaning two letters that spell one sound. Lh is [ʎ], like the lli of million (milhares). Nh is [ɲ], like the ny of canyon (minha, vizinho, manhã, amanhã). Ch is [ʃ], the sh of shoe (chuva, riacho, manchete). Rr is the strong r, the same sound as a single r at the start of a word (carro). Ss is [s]; it is doubled because a single s between two vowels would be [z], so sessenta and assembleia need ss to keep the hiss. H is always silent (hoje, humanidade, hospital). The sequence sh does not exist in native Portuguese words; shopping is an English loan word and keeps its English sound [ʃ].

Qu and gu. Before e or i the u is silent and only makes the consonant hard: que, quem, quinhentos, português (por-tu-GUÊS). Before a or o the u is pronounced as a glide [w]: quase, quatro, quantos, qualquer, água. A few words pronounce the u even before e or i, and they must be learned: cinquenta, frequente, tranquilo. A g before u is the hard g, as in inaugurar.

X and s. The prefix ex before a vowel is [z]: exato, exigir, existir. An s that ends a syllable before a voiceless consonant (p, t, c, f, q) is [s], and before a voiced one (b, d, g, v, m, n, l, r) it is [z], as in desde and mesmo. In Rio de Janeiro and some other regions these are [ʃ] and [ʒ]. Descoberta is des-co-BER-ta, with the s closing des and the c before o as [k], and estão is es-TÃO. The letter j is always [ʒ], the s of measure (projetada, jesuítas, jornal).

T, d, the final vowels, nasals and l. In most of Brazil, before i and before an unstressed final e (which is said like i), t is [tʃ] and d is [dʒ]: ponte, manchete, notícia, cidade, humanidade, edifício. A vowel followed by m or n that closes its syllable is nasal, and the m or n is not pronounced as a consonant: ponte, sendo, mundo, quantos, fundar, inventar, manchete, condomínio. An n that opens a syllable is an ordinary consonant, and the vowel before it is only lightly nasal: in ce-ri-MÔ-ni-a the n is said as in English knee. G before e or i is [ʒ] and before a, o or u it is [g]: garagem has both, ga-RA-gem. An l that ends a syllable, including a final l, is [w]: hospital, jornal, Planalto, Alvorada. A final r is weak and often dropped in speech, so inaugurar, construir and descobrir end in a vowel sound.

Vowel pairs. Foreign names such as Wright, Dumont and Niemeyer keep their original spelling, and Portuguese speakers adapt the sounds. Ei is [ej], as in lei and assembleia. Ou is said [o] in everyday speech (voou, mudou, ficou). Ai is [aj] (mais, principais). Oi is [oj] (noite). These are the diphthongs of the sounds lesson; they are one syllable each.

grammar.title: Voice: the doer, the receiver and five ways to say who acts
grammar.explanation:
Every sentence about an event has, in principle, two roles: the doer and the receiver. Grammar names them with terms you already know. The subject is the person or thing the verb is about, and the direct object (from the object pronoun lesson) is what receives the action without a preposition: in O porteiro abriu a porta, porteiro is the subject and porta is the direct object. A verb that can take a direct object is called transitive. A verb that cannot is called intransitive: dormir, chegar and viver stand alone, and precisar de and gostar de keep a preposition between the verb and what follows, so what follows is not a direct object.

Voice says which role the subject plays. In the active voice the subject is the doer: O porteiro abriu a porta. In the passive voice the subject is the receiver, and the doer, called the agent, appears afterwards with por or does not appear at all: A porta foi aberta pelo porteiro, or simply A porta foi aberta. The passive is a rearrangement of the active sentence: the old direct object becomes the subject, and the old subject becomes the agent. This is why only transitive verbs have a passive. Nothing can be moved to subject position if there was no direct object.

Why would anyone leave out the doer? Because it is unknown (someone stole my phone), unimportant (the bridge was opened), obvious (tickets are sold at the ticket office), or better left unsaid. News, law, science and history are also about things more than people, so the thing becomes the subject. That is why the vocabulary of this unit is about headlines, rules, deadlines and inventions.

English has one main tool for this, be plus a participle (the door was opened), together with the vague they (they stole my phone) and one or you (you never know). Portuguese has five tools, and each belongs to a different situation. The ser passive is the formal, written one. The passive se is the tool of signs and rules. The impersonal se is for statements with no subject at all. The third person plural without a pronoun says that some unnamed people did something. A gente and você make general statements that include the speaker or anyone. The next notes take them one at a time. The table shows all five on one idea.

There is one important limit that English does not share. In English the receiver can be the indirect object: I was given a book, she was told the news. In Portuguese only a direct object can become the subject of a ser passive, because an indirect object keeps its preposition. You cannot say Eu fui dado um livro. You say Me deram um livro, with the third person plural (they gave me a book), and Me disseram que o prazo acabou for I was told that the deadline is over. The same holds for verbs that keep a preposition: nobody turns confiar em alguém into a passive.

grammar.title: The passive with ser + participle + por
grammar.explanation:
The recipe. Take an active sentence, make its direct object the subject, put ser in the tense the active verb had, add the past participle of the main verb, and introduce the old subject with por. Active: O arquiteto desenhou a cidade. Passive: A cidade foi desenhada pelo arquiteto. The tense moves to ser, and the participle carries the meaning. English builds its passive the same way with be plus a participle, so the logic transfers. What Portuguese adds is agreement. The participle works like an adjective, as the participle lesson explained, so it agrees in gender and number with the new subject: a casa foi construída, os prédios foram construídos. English built never changes.

Only ser changes for tense and mood. Because sendo is the gerund of ser, the progressive is estar sendo plus the participle. Ser appears as an infinitive after helper verbs, meaning verbs such as ir, dever, poder and precisar that are followed by an infinitive, and after prepositions (A lei vai ser votada, As bicicletas devem ser guardadas, depois de ser construída). It also has its own future (será aprovada) and subjunctive (exige que sejam entregues). The participle stays the same in every case; only its ending agrees with the subject. Be careful with foi, which is the preterite of both ser and ir; the participle after it shows that it is ser.

The agent is introduced by por, and por fuses with the articles as the places lesson showed: por + o = pelo, por + a = pela, por + os = pelos, por + as = pelas. Before a noun with no article, or with um and uma, por stays separate: por jesuítas, por uma equipe. The agent is often left out when it is unknown or does not matter: A ponte foi inaugurada ontem.

Which tense of ser? It follows the meaning of the active verb. A finished event takes foi, a repeated event in the past takes era, and a plan takes será or vai ser. The present é aprovada describes a regular event (every year the budget is approved) more often than something happening now; for something in progress use estar sendo. Several participles are irregular or double, as the participle lesson showed: feito, dito, escrito, aberto, reaberto, descoberto, posto and visto; and with ser the short forms are used: foi aceito, foi entregue, foi eleito.

Portuguese vocabulary has false friends here: realizar means to carry out or hold (a reunião será realizada), not to realize in the sense of notice.

How often is it used? The ser passive is the standard of news, law, history and official notices. In conversation Brazilians prefer the active voice, the third person plural or se. Headlines often drop ser altogether, leaving the participle alone: Projeto aprovado no Senado. That is the same bare participle as Feito! or Resolvido!

grammar.title: The pronoun se: passive and impersonal
grammar.explanation:
The problem it solves. Sometimes you want a passive but the ser passive feels heavy, as on a sign. Portuguese has a lighter tool: se next to a third person verb. The reflexive lesson taught se as oneself: Ela se veste means she dresses herself. The passive se grows from the same idea. Vende-se casa is literally sells-itself house, that is, the house sells itself, which in practice means it is for sale. No doer is named, and the thing itself becomes the subject.

There are two uses, and one question tells them apart: does the verb have a direct object, a noun with no preposition in front of it? If it does, that noun is the subject and the verb agrees with it. This is the passive se: Vende-se casa (one house), Vendem-se casas (several), Aluga-se quarto, Alugam-se quartos, Fala-se inglês, Falam-se duas línguas. In Vendem-se casas the subject is casas, which is why the verb is plural: houses sell themselves.

If the verb has no direct object, there is no subject to agree with, so the verb is always third person singular. This is the impersonal se. It is the case with verbs that keep a preposition (precisar de, gostar de, cuidar de), with intransitive verbs (trabalhar, viver, chegar) and with ser and estar. Precisa-se de motoristas means needs-itself of drivers. The phrase de motoristas is a prepositional phrase, that is, a preposition with its noun, and not a subject, so a plural noun there cannot make the verb plural. Compare Trabalha-se muito aqui and Vive-se bem no interior. The pattern also covers a helper verb followed by an infinitive: Não se pode fumar aqui and Pode-se pagar com cartão. The helper verb stays singular, because what is possible is the whole act of smoking or paying. The same goes for Diz-se que ela foi feita para os carros (it is said that it was made for cars), where the thing said is the whole clause that follows (a clause is a group of words with its own verb).

Where does se go? In speech and informal writing before the verb: Aqui se fala português, Nesta casa se fala português. On signs and in formal writing it follows the verb with a hyphen when the verb starts the clause: Vende-se, Vendem-se, Precisa-se. After não, que, onde and other such words it goes before the verb even in careful writing: Não se pode mudar, o lugar onde se vende.

Spoken and informal usage. Many Brazilians write Aluga-se quartos and Vende-se casas, with a singular verb before a plural noun, because they feel se as an impersonal marker. Formal grammar treats this as an error. When you write carefully, make the verb agree with the thing: Alugam-se quartos.

Two cautions. First, se also means oneself and each other, so a sentence with a person as the thing acted on can be ambiguous: Mataram-se os soldados could mean the soldiers killed themselves. For people, choose the ser passive or the third person plural: Os soldados foram mortos. Second, the passive se cannot have an agent. You cannot add pelo dono to Vende-se casa. If you need an agent, use ser plus por.

grammar.title: Estar + participle: a result, not an action
grammar.explanation:
The principle. Ser plus a participle describes an event, which is the passive voice from the previous note. Estar plus a participle describes the state that the event leaves behind. A porta foi aberta tells of the act of opening. A porta está aberta says only that the door is now open, and does not say who opened it or when. The choice of verb follows the ser and estar lesson: ser for what happens or defines, estar for a condition at a time.

English often uses different words for the state and the event (the door is open, the door was opened), so the two ideas look different. Portuguese has one form for both: aberta is the participle of abrir and also the word for open, and fechada is the participle of fechar and also the word for closed. Like any adjective, the participle agrees with the noun: a loja está fechada, os documentos estão guardados, as vagas estão preenchidas.

Two tests. Can you add an agent with por? If so, you need ser: A porta foi aberta pelo porteiro, but not A porta está aberta pelo porteiro. Can you add já or agora? If so, you probably want estar: A porta já está aberta.

Three variants are worth separating. Estar sendo plus the participle is the process in progress: A ponte está sendo construída means builders are working on it now, while A ponte está construída means it is finished. Ficar plus a participle is a state that comes about or is standing: A loja ficou fechada o dia todo, O museu fica fechado às segundas-feiras. And the ser passive in the present (A loja é fechada às seis) describes a repeated action by someone, which is rare in speech.

This pattern is everywhere on signs, where the verb is dropped altogether: Fechado para reforma, Aberto, Esgotado, Interditado, Reservado. In Brazil you also see Em obras. Many common adjectives are participles that became ordinary adjectives: cansado, preocupado, casado, parado. Notice also that the participle after ter does not agree (Ela tem aberto as portas), but after ser, estar and ficar it does (As portas estão abertas).

grammar.title: Unspecified subjects: third person plural, a gente and você
grammar.explanation:
The principle. The ending of a Portuguese verb already says person and number, so a third person plural verb with no stated subject is a complete sentence, and it points to some people who are not named: Roubaram meu celular, Bateram na porta, Fecharam a rua. English needs the pronoun they for this, even though they is not anybody in particular. Portuguese has no pronoun, and the contrast matters. Adding eles changes the meaning to a specific group already in the conversation: Eles roubaram meu celular means those people did it.

Hearsay, meaning news passed on from other people, is the most common use. Dizem que, Falam que, Falaram no rádio que and Me disseram que all pass on news with no source, and they are often more natural than a passive. Saiu na TV que (it came out on TV that) works the same way. The speaker signals that the information comes from somewhere else and takes no responsibility for it.

General statements that include the speaker use a gente or você. A gente paga muito imposto aqui means we, the people who live here, pay a lot of tax. Você nunca sabe o que vai acontecer uses você to mean anyone, which is why it is not addressed to the listener in particular. Both take a third person singular verb, as a gente and você always do. Todo mundo (everybody) is also singular: todo mundo sabe. English makes the same choices among one, you and we, but Brazilians seldom say the equivalent of one. The se construction is mostly a writing device: Paga-se muito imposto aqui is formal, while A gente paga muito imposto is what people say.

Compare the tools: a third person plural implies that some doers exist, while se names no doer at all. Falam português aqui reads as people here speak Portuguese, and Fala-se português aqui is the sign. One trap remains. A third person plural verb with no subject can also be a dropped eles that refers to a group already mentioned: Os vizinhos saíram. Disseram que voltam logo. Context decides.

culture.title: Placas, avisos e o jeito brasileiro de avisar
culture.text:
Everyday life in Brazil is full of signs, and most of them use exactly the constructions in this unit. On building fronts you see Aluga-se and Vende-se, often with a phone number written by hand. Job ads say Precisa-se de, and shop windows announce Fechado para balanço (closed for stocktaking, literally closed for balance) or Em obras (under construction, literally in works). In the street you find Proibido estacionar, Saída de veículos and Cuidado com o degrau (care with the step). Learning to read these quickly is one of the most practical skills for a visitor.

Brazilian notices also have their own tone. A written warning on a condominium door is often polite and indirect: Favor não deixar objetos no corredor (literally favor, not to leave objects in the hallway), or Pedimos a gentileza de manter o silêncio após as vinte e duas horas (we ask the kindness of keeping silence after ten p.m.). Shops thank you for coming with Obrigado pela preferência (thanks for the preference). There is a long tradition of humorous signs too, such as Fiado só amanhã, which promises credit tomorrow and so never.

The news uses the passive heavily. Headlines are short and often drop the verb ser: Projeto aprovado no Senado, Ponte será inaugurada na sexta. In conversation, though, people pass on news with Dizem que, Falaram que or Saiu na TV que (it came out on TV that). If you understand both styles, you can follow a newspaper and the chat in a bakery queue.

paragraphs.pt: Brasília é uma das poucas capitais do mundo que foram planejadas antes de existir. A cidade foi inaugurada em mil novecentos e sessenta, depois de ser construída em menos de cinco anos.
paragraphs.en: Brasília is one of the few capitals in the world that were planned before they existed. The city was inaugurated in 1960, after being built in less than five years.

paragraphs.pt: O projeto urbanístico foi feito por Lúcio Costa, e os principais edifícios foram desenhados por Oscar Niemeyer. Tudo foi construído no meio do Planalto Central.
paragraphs.en: The urban plan was made by Lúcio Costa, and the main buildings were designed by Oscar Niemeyer. Everything was built in the middle of the Central Plateau.

paragraphs.pt: Em mil novecentos e oitenta e sete, o centro da cidade foi declarado patrimônio da humanidade pela UNESCO. Desde então, a área é protegida por regras rígidas.
paragraphs.en: In 1987, the city center was declared a World Heritage Site by UNESCO. Since then, the area has been protected by strict rules.
paragraphs.literal: In thousand nine-hundred and eighty and seven, the center of-the city was declared heritage of-the humanity by-the UNESCO. Since then, the area is protected by rules rigid.

paragraphs.literal: Not itself can change the height of-the buildings, and any new construction needs to-be approved by an agency special. For this, the landscape almost not changed.

paragraphs.pt: Apesar da fama, a cidade também é criticada. Diz-se que ela foi feita para os carros, e não para as pessoas, e muitos moradores reclamam das grandes distâncias.

paragraphs.pt: Mesmo assim, o Plano Piloto é visitado todos os anos por milhares de turistas. A Catedral e o Palácio da Alvorada estão abertos ao público em dias determinados.

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between 'A ponte está construída' and 'A ponte está sendo construída'?

exercises.prompt: In 'Dizem que o preço vai subir', who is the subject of dizem?

exercises.prompt: Which sentence points to a specific group of people already mentioned in the conversation?

exercises.prompt: Why does notícia carry an accent while confiança does not?
choices: Notícia is feminine and confiança is not
Notícia ends in a glide plus a vowel, so it is stressed on the third to last syllable, while confiança is stressed on the second to last, as its ending predicts
Confiança has a cedilla, which replaces the accent
exercises.explanation: The accent appears when the stress breaks the default of the ending. In no-TÍ-ci-a the ia counts as two syllables, so the stress is third to last. In con-fi-AN-ça the stress is where the ending a predicts.

exercises.prompt: Why is there an accent on the í of construída?
choices: Because the word is stressed on the last syllable
Because the word is a noun
Because the u and the í are two separate syllables, a hiatus, and the accent keeps them apart
Because the ending a needs a mark
exercises.explanation: The pair u-í is not a diphthong. The accent on the stressed í marks the hiatus: cons-tru-Í-da.

exercises.prompt: Why is the x said [z] in exigir?
choices: Because there is a silent h
Because the next letter is g
Because the prefix ex before a vowel is [z]
exercises.explanation: The letter x has several values, including [ʃ], [s], [ks] and [z]. The prefix ex before a vowel is [z], as in exato and existir.

exercises.prompt: Why does patrimônio have a circumflex while médico has an acute?
choices: Both are stressed on the third to last syllable, but the o of patrimônio is closed before n, while the e of médico is open
Patrimônio is a noun and médico is an adjective
Patrimônio ends in o and médico also ends in o
The circumflex marks a nasal diphthong
exercises.explanation: A stressed vowel before n is closed, so the circumflex. In médico the stressed e is open, so the acute.

exercises.prompt_pt: A Universidade de São Paulo ___ fundada em mil novecentos e trinta e quatro.
exercises.hint_en: The University of São Paulo was founded in 1934.
exercises.explanation: A completed past event takes the preterite of ser, which agrees with the subject: a Universidade, third person singular.

exercises.prompt_pt: Esses livros foram escritos ___ autora mais famosa do país.
exercises.hint_en: These books were written by the most famous author in the country.
exercises.explanation: Por introduces the agent, and por + a contracts to pela.
The participle agrees with the feminine plural subject as leis: aprovadas.

exercises.prompt_pt: Ontem a porta ___ aberta pelo porteiro.
exercises.hint_en: Yesterday the door was opened by the doorman.
exercises.explanation: The agent pelo porteiro shows that this is an event, so ser is needed.
Agora and the absence of an agent point to a state, so estar plus the participle.

exercises.prompt_pt: As bicicletas devem ___ guardadas na garagem.
exercises.hint_en: Bicycles must be kept in the garage.
exercises.explanation: After a helper verb such as dever, the passive uses the infinitive ser plus the participle.

exercises.hint_en: House at the beach for sale.
exercises.explanation: Vender takes a direct object, and casa is singular, so the passive se goes with a singular verb, after the verb with a hyphen as on signs.
The verb is plural because bicicletas is the plural subject of the passive se.

exercises.prompt_pt: Precisa-___ de pessoas com experiência em vendas.
exercises.explanation: Impersonal se with precisar de: there is no direct object, so the verb stays singular.

exercises.hint_en: The bridge is still being built.
exercises.explanation: The progressive passive is estar plus sendo plus the participle.

exercises.hint_en: They say the price is going to go up.
exercises.explanation: The usual way to pass on hearsay is the third person plural with no pronoun. Diz-se que is the formal impersonal equivalent.
Ser in the preterite plus the feminine singular participle.

answers: O português é falado no Brasil.
exercises.explanation: Either the passive se with a singular object or the ser passive.
A state, so estar plus the participle, agreeing with a loja.

exercises.prompt_en: The new library is being built.
answers: A nova biblioteca está sendo construída.
A biblioteca nova está sendo construída.
exercises.explanation: A process in progress: estar sendo plus the participle.
Ingressos is the plural subject, so the verb is plural with se, and the participle is masculine plural in the ser passive.

exercises.prompt_en: They say the street is closed off.
answers: Dizem que a rua está interditada.
Falam que a rua está interditada.
Dizem que a rua está fechada.
Falam que a rua está fechada.
exercises.explanation: Hearsay uses the third person plural with no pronoun, and the closed street is a state.
